statement: Sara has plenty of 2-euro coins and 5-euro notes, and no other money. She wants to pay exactly 23 euros without getting any change. What is the smallest total number of coins and notes she can use?

choices.misconception: I counted only the 5-euro notes and forgot to add the coins.
I counted only the 2-euro coins and forgot to add the notes.
I used as many notes as possible, four of them, and then two coins, without checking that this makes 24 euros, not 23.
I used one note and nine coins, the first way I found, and did not look for a way with fewer pieces.

hints: Can she use an even number of 5-euro notes?
Try each possible number of 5-euro notes and check whether the rest can be paid in 2-euro coins. Then compare the totals and keep the smallest.
The coins always make an even amount, so the notes must make an odd amount: 1 note or 3 notes. With 3 notes, 8 euros are left, which is 4 coins.

solutions.reliable: The 2-euro coins always add up to an even number of euros, and 23 is odd, so the 5-euro notes must make an odd amount: 1 note (5 euros) or 3 notes (15 euros). With 1 note, 18 euros are left, which needs 9 coins, so 10 pieces. With 3 notes, 8 euros are left, which needs 4 coins, so 7 pieces. Four notes would already be 20, leaving 3 euros that coins cannot make. The smallest number is 7. The transferable idea: use parity to cut down the cases before you count.

whyOnTest: Money problems at 3 points check that you test every combination, not just the greedy one.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
